title: Universities need a skills ecosystem mindset
summary: Sammy Shummo argues that universities need to move beyond course portfolios and build coherent skills ecosystems
full_text:
Universities are very good at talking about portfolios.

We review them, validate them, market them, monitor them and occasionally close parts of them. But too often, the conversation still starts in the wrong place.

It starts with the institution. It starts with the course we want to run, the market we think exists, the recruitment target we need to hit, the academic expertise we already have, or the financial contribution we hope the programme will make. All of those things matter. But they are not the starting point for a serious skills strategy.

Making the first move

The starting point should be the workforce problem.

Employers rarely approach universities, colleges or training providers with a neat qualification request. They don’t usually begin by asking for a degree apprenticeship, a Higher Technical Qualification, a CPD course, a T Level placement or a short unit of learning.

They begin with a business problem. They need to recruit, retain, reskill, improve productivity, develop managers, respond to AI, decarbonise operations, strengthen social value, or create a future talent pipeline.

The role of a university should be to translate those workforce problems into high-quality learning solutions. That requires a different way of thinking about portfolio development.

The skills evidence is now too strong to ignore. Skills England’s 2026 Annual Skills Report makes clear that the system needs to be more evidence-led and aligned to priority sectors. The Employer Skills Survey 2024 reported 250,500 skill-shortage vacancies across the UK. It also showed that employer training expenditure was £53 billion in 2024, down from £59 billion in 2022 and 18.5 per cent lower in real terms than in 2011.

This tells us two things. Employers still need skills, but we cannot assume that need will automatically convert into investment in training. The offer has to be relevant, flexible and easy to navigate.

That is where universities need to move from course portfolio management to skills ecosystem leadership.

The ecosystem question

A course portfolio is a list of provision.

A skills ecosystem is a set of relationships, pathways, and capabilities that connect learners, employers, colleges, universities, professional bodies, and local economies.

The first asks: what can we teach? The second asks: what does the economy need, what do learners need, and what can we deliver well?

This shift matters because the skills challenge is not limited to apprenticeships. Apprenticeships are important, but they are only one part of the answer. Employers also need placements, internships, graduate recruitment, CPD, professional education, short courses, apprenticeship units, Higher Technical Qualifications and applied research.

And learners need progression routes, not disconnected products.

For universities, this has implications for how we work with employers. Business engagement cannot sit at the edge of the institution as a sales or recruitment function. It has to become a source of strategic intelligence.

Employer-facing teams hear things that should shape institutional decisions: where demand is growing, where employers are struggling to recruit, which delivery models do not work, where curriculum is behind practice, and what skills are emerging in the workplace. If that intelligence stays in individual inboxes or relationship notes, the institution does not learn from it.

A mature business engagement function should generate opportunities, but it should also inform portfolio development. It should help universities decide what to grow, what to redesign, what to stop, and where to partner.

Finding the right path

This also means universities need to think in pathways.

A pathway is not the same as a course. A pathway connects school engagement, technical education, placements, apprenticeships, higher technical learning, degrees, CPD and professional progression.

It makes sense to employers because it supports workforce planning. It makes sense to learners because it creates visible routes into and through work.

This is where integrated education groups have a particular opportunity. At LSBU Group, for example, the combination of London South Bank University, South Bank Colleges and South Bank Academies creates the potential to connect early talent, technical education, higher education, apprenticeships, placements and professional learning. The wider lesson is not institutional self-promotion. It’s that structures only become valuable when they simplify the journey for employers and strengthen progression for learners.

A construction employer does not want to navigate separate parts of an institution to discuss school outreach or graduate recruitment. A health employer does not want disconnected conversations about nursing associates, registered nurses, allied health, placements and leadership development. The employer wants a coherent workforce conversation and universities need to organise themselves accordingly.

Quality street

There is also a quality point. Flexible provision must not mean weaker provision.

Shorter courses, modular learning and apprenticeship units can help employers respond quickly to change, especially in areas such as AI, digital, green skills and leadership. But if they become disconnected fragments, they will add complexity rather than solve it. Quality has to be designed across the whole skills ecosystem.

For apprenticeships, that means robust initial assessment, employer commitment, progress reviews, and assessment readiness. For placements, it means meaningful workplace learning, not just hours completed. In terms of CPD, it means learning that can be applied in practice. And in higher technical provision, it means employer recognition and progression value.

The same principle applies to impact. Universities are used to measuring enrolments, income, and continuation. Those are important, but they are not enough. A skills ecosystem approach requires us to measure employer satisfaction, repeat engagement, learner progression, placement outcomes, social mobility, productivity contribution and regional value. This is not about turning universities into training suppliers. It is about taking seriously our role as civic and economic institutions.

Universities remain places of knowledge, research, critique and intellectual development. But if we are serious about public value, we must also be serious about how that knowledge connects to work, opportunity and place.

The next phase of skills reform will reward institutions that can join things up. Not those with the longest list of courses. Not those with the most polished prospectus. Not even those with the loudest employer engagement rhetoric. The strongest institutions will be those that can build skills ecosystems: coherent, employer-informed, learner-centred, and rooted in place.

That requires universities to ask harder questions of their portfolios. Not only: does this course recruit? But also: what problem does it solve? Which employers helped shape it?

How does it connect to progression? Can working adults access it? Is the delivery model viable? What impact will it have?

That’s the shift we now need to make. Portfolio development should not just decide which courses run. It should design the skills infrastructure that employers, learners, and communities need.

title: What do the OfS’ new risk categories really tell us about financial viability
summary: Matthew Howling outlines the gap between what the Office for Students' framework says and what its risk categories might mean for providers under financial pressure
full_text:
Over the summer, the Office for Students (OfS) announced a new risk assessment framework intended to guide the regulator’s assessments of providers’ financial viability and sustainability.

Setting out an approach in this way addresses an implied demand for consistency and transparency in exercising regulatory judgement – understandable when the stakes are so high for providers facing financial difficulty. What the framework does not do, is change OfS’ powers of intervention in cases of providers whose financial resilience and sustainability is judged to be at significant risk. Only a change in the law can change OfS’ enforcement powers.

The distinction is an important one because there is a risk that third party stakeholders start using OfS’ framework and, more specifically, OfS’s risk categories, as trigger events for their own enforcement powers.

OfS’ powers are relatively limited – although “pausing OfS funding in the interests of protecting public funding” is one of the interventions which providers might expect from the regulator if they are assessed as being in Category 4/“Acute financial concerns.” If, at the same time, a Category 4 assessment triggered a lender to demand early repayment, the result could feasibly be to tip providers into insolvency.

Risk based regulation

Under the new framework, OfS will place providers into one of five risk categories, ranging from Category 1/“No financial concerns” to Category 5/“Market exit.” This approach offers a marked contrast to the regulatory framework overall, which states in para 126 that OfS will not assign an overall summative risk rating or classification to an individual provider. While that statement is probably still true in a strict sense – the new risk categories are only looking at financial risk – the express acknowledgment that these categories exist and that they are assessing the topic which is on everyone’s lips at the moment is surely going to pique some interest.

OfS lists five different financial metrics that it will be looking at together with non-financial metrics – for example, capital expenditure requirements, headroom on lending covenants and refinancing risk. Banks and other lenders might typically focus on a slightly smaller number of metrics. Clearly (and understandably) OfS wants to give the impression that it is taking a broader view to account for institutional diversity and context.

Crucially, OfS is not publishing the thresholds for each metric. Whether that is the right approach is a question for chief financial officers and finance professionals to consider. The answer, I suspect, is likely to depend on how the metrics are used and the debates that are likely to ensue between the regulator and individual providers about what the “right” number might look like. At present, we have no visibility on how many providers might currently be in each category.

Categorical consequences

In addition to the financial indicators, the framework also sets out the “typical” financial characteristics in each category and a description of what providers can expect from their regulator in terms of monitoring, engagement, and intervention in each risk category.

Providers in Category 1/“No financial concerns”) or Category 2/“Possible financial concerns” can largely sleep soundly at night. OfS tells us:

“Providers in categories 1 and 2 should expect engagement…to be minimal and limited to routine regulatory interactions, with no enhanced monitoring or additional regulatory intervention unless new risks emerge.”

Providers in Categories 3 /“Actual financial concerns” and 4/“Acute financial concerns” won’t be so lucky. In those situations, OfS will communicate with the accountable officer and chair of the governing body to discuss OfS’ judgement and what that will mean in terms of further action.

Providers in Category 4 can typically expect a Student Protection Direction (SPD) to be in their immediate future. We have previously explained why SPDs aren’t necessarily fit for purpose in the real world. The concern, more generally, is that with a regulator who, as the framework is at pains to point out, “does not have a duty, or powers, to manage a provider’s financial risk, or prevent a provider from closing” any intervention and monitoring as a result of being placed in Categories 3 or 4 is essentially going to be a data gathering exercise. This will add to providers’ burdens at the very point where the attention of finance and senior leadership teams should be focused on turning around the institution.

Private matter and public interest

Beyond regulatory consequentials, it remains unknown how lenders and other stakeholders – such as pension funds – are going to react to this. In a sense, the framework is nothing new. Back in the day, HEFCE would carry out risk assessments based on a provider’s annual accountability returns. The risk assessment would be reported to the governing body and the accountable officer. There were two risk categories: “not at higher risk” (the vast majority of higher education institutions) and “at higher risk” (a small minority).

There was a support strategy for institutions at higher risk and, in exceptional circumstances, HEFCE could make an “at higher risk” assessment public where it considered it to be in the collective interest of students or the public to do so. In addition, HEFCE would consider withdrawing the grant in full or in part. Those risk assessments often found their way, contractually, into lender’s loan agreements, either as reporting obligations or, more seriously, as events of default. Risk assessments have also been a tool of OfS since its inception.

Indeed, under section 7(1) of the 2017 Higher Education and Research Act OfS is under a statutory duty to “ensure that the initial registration conditions applicable to an institution and its ongoing registration conditions are proportionate to the OfS’s assessment of the regulatory risk posed by the institution.” So, it has always been OfS’ job to assess a provider’s regulatory risk. “Regulatory risk” is defined in section 7(2) as “the risk of the institution, when it is registered, failing to comply with regulation by the OfS.”

However, risk assessments were a private matter. The continuation of this convention, and its rationale, was set out explicitly in OfS’ regulatory framework:

The OfS does not intend to publish its risk assessments or the risk profiles for individual providers. Such information could be erroneously treated as equivalent to judgements on a provider’s quality and have an unnecessary reputational impact. Publication could in fact be harmful to the OfS’s ability to carry out its regulatory functions, for example, by creating confusion, giving providers insights that allow them a commercial advantage, or affecting the OfS’s ongoing relationships with providers.

OfS was also fairly sketchy about what metrics it was looking at, at least from the point of view of financial risk. There are specific conditions of registration around being financially viable and financially sustainable – with specific meanings attributed to those phrases – but the detail of the indicators that OfS was using to assess those things was not widely publicised.

In 2020, the height of the pandemic, OfS introduced a new reportable event where it was “reasonably likely that liquidity will drop below 30 days at any point during a rolling three-month period.” During the Covid era providers started to need financial covenant amendments and waivers from their lenders so in 2022, Regulatory Advice 16 includes within its list of events that is always reportable “a likely breach of any financial covenant attached to a loan, where that breach has not been waived by the lender.”

The regulator’s language is slightly wobbly here – what does “likely” mean in this context and does “waived” mean that you have to have breached it first ie before the waiver is issued?

Nevertheless, there was a sense in which – apart from the liquidity test – OfS was content to piggyback off the covenants imposed contractually by lenders. Conceptually, that’s not necessarily a bad idea. If OfS was applying financial metrics to individual providers, then it was doing so privately as part of its own internal risk assessments. Bringing those internal risk assessments out into the open (or at least telling the world that it will be entering into a dialogue with individual providers about their individual risk assessments) does feel like a move back to a more HEFCE-style of approach.

Given the financial headwinds facing the sector, it is not surprising that OfS is trying to demonstrate that its financial oversight is operating at an individual provider level, not just at the level of assessing the financial sustainability of the sector as a whole. However, the new issue which the framework creates is that lenders are going to be extremely interested in hearing whether their borrowers have been placed in Category 3 or Category 4.

OfS acknowledges this in paragraph 42 of the framework:

We are aware that affected providers will have obligations to third parties, such as lenders and others with a financial interest, about the disclosure of regulatory actions. The OfS has no expectation that institutions provide stakeholders with copies of our regulatory decisions. However, we understand that lenders and others with a financial interest may expect providers in category 4 that are in receipt of a material risk of market exit assessment and/or a Student Protection Direction to share relevant information with them. Conversely, we do not believe third parties should need providers to supply them with a copy of any F3 Notices the OfS has issued. In all cases, it remains the provider’s responsibility to determine the extent of any disclosure, considering their specific circumstances and contractual obligations.

However, in my view, the regulator is perhaps being slightly naive here. If OfS has made an evidence-based assessment that a provider has actual or acute financial concerns, then it is surely not unreasonable of a major creditor (such as a bank or pension fund) to want to know about that assessment and what the regulator is doing about it.

Whatever contractual rights lenders have at the moment in terms of disclosure of regulatory action, lenders may well feel compelled to write a disclosure obligation – whereby, for example, the university must tell the lender if it is moved into Category 3 or Category 4 – into future facility agreements.

Existing arrangements are also not necessarily immune given the number of amendments and waivers that are currently being sought by the sector (“we’ll give you that extra covenant headroom, but we want to know if you are in Category 3”). It can only be hoped that lenders (and their lawyers) are measured about this.

While OfS has no remit or powers to prevent a provider from closing, the regulator is (one would hope) itself unlikely to tip a provider into insolvency: its powers are essentially that of a monitor and overseer, not a rival creditor. Ultimately, its risk assessments should not be revealing anything that an engaged lender doesn’t know about already.

Nevertheless, including a contractual event of default in a loan agreement around a provider being placed in Category 4 runs the risk of accelerating the problem that a prudent financial monitoring regime was presumably intended to avoid.

This article is published as part of a partnership with Mills & Reeve.

title: Five things I’ve learned from five young men applying to university this year
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Lucy Haire, Director of Sector Engagement at UPP, writing in a personal capacity. This year, my son was in Year 13 at an impressively well-run central London comprehensive boys’ school, and he and his friends were in the thick of applying to university. Working for a student accommodation company, […]

The post Five things I’ve learned from five young men applying to university this year appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Lucy Haire, Director of Sector Engagement at UPP, writing in a personal capacity.

This year, my son was in Year 13 at an impressively well-run central London comprehensive boys’ school, and he and his friends were in the thick of applying to university. Working for a student accommodation company, and previously for the Higher Education Policy Institute, alongside my early-career background as a sixth-form teacher who oversaw hundreds of UCAS forms, I’m familiar with university admissions. Yet supporting my son and some of his close friends revealed the reality of a process that is far more complex, time-consuming and demanding than many parents and carers might imagine.

1. Few know what they want to study.

In my sample of prospective students, only one really knew what he wanted to study. University departments and careers services put immense effort into open days, talks, taster sessions and social media content, but the young men I spoke to were still unsure. Apart from the one student who was completely certain, the rest simply half-liked some subjects and wondered about others before taking a leap of faith. In fact, one young man asked for help switching to a completely different subject just days before the deadline. Fortunately, UCAS (the UK’s university application service) makes this relatively straightforward. Another had no idea what to pick and was ready to give up, but I worked with him through the night to find suitable courses and submit his application in time for the next day’s deadline. While my sample may not be representative, it could reflect the reality that hundreds of thousands of students are rolling up to higher education this autumn on sheer faith.

2. Apprenticeships are seen as the holy grail – but are very hard to come by.

All but one of the young men I was talking to repeatedly said that they wanted an apprenticeship, imbibing near-propaganda level promotion from recent governments, with their school dutifully covering the ground. But securing one proved very hard. Unlike university applications, apprenticeship admissions are mostly run by individual organisations on their own timetables, and places are far scarcer. One student did everything right: relevant work experience, top performance on company tests and in interviews, great predicted grades and exemplary manners. Coming from a modest working-class background, he was still unsuccessful and ultimately accepted a place at a Russell Group university instead.

3. Applying for a student loan can be difficult.

Supporting all five students with their applications was just the first step. As offers rolled in, I checked if they were accepting them and considering student loans and accommodation. During peak exam season, one student missed the loan deadline and hadn’t arranged housing. He had emailed his preferred university requesting an administrative number needed for his loan application, but received no reply. I called the switchboard for him and was passed between departments, none of which had the answer. I insisted until they eventually found it. This particular university came dangerously close to losing the student in the process.

4. Re-sits are a mystery.

No one talks about re-sits. Information evenings focus on UCAS Clearing and Confirmation, which is great for finding alternative courses, but never mention retaking A levels. One student reached out to me (this student was not in my original group of five supportees), unsure of her options after missing her grades. Schools naturally focus on first-time success, and there can be barriers to retaking exams at your own school. But seeing the whites of the eyes of this student and her parents who had realised re-sits were their best path but have no idea where to turn shows a gap in support.

5. Clearing experiences vary, and it really shows.

One young man performed brilliantly in his marketing BTEC and applied for related degrees in London, but returned after results day determined to study philosophy instead. His family couldn’t guide him, so, admittedly nervous about his new idea, I spent time checking his motivation and whether he understood the demands of a non-vocational subject. Satisfied with his resolve, we explored options and he secured two Clearing offers. To help him decide, I called both universities and arranged for him to attend their open afternoons that week. One institution offered only a generic campus tour without subject details or academic staff, whereas the other had a philosophy lecturer lead the tour, right in the middle of the summer recess. You can guess which university he chose.

What to make of it all?

Having worked around higher education for over 15 years and in education generally for even longer, I remain deeply impressed by those who teach, create courses and handle the administrative and leadership demands of schools and universities. I’ve written for HEPI before about the complexity of a vice-chancellor’s role, and I view school headteachers in much the same light: nearly all deserve far more praise than the public or press are willing to give. This blog isn’t a detailed policy report based on carefully analysed surveys of thousands of applicants or dozens of parent focus groups, all of which make for fantastic repositories of evidence. Rather, it’s a snapshot of a group of young men, some of whom are first-generation university applicants, others not; some are from middle-class backgrounds, others more disadvantaged; some second-generation migrants, others not.

I’ve recorded this simply as a reflection of how I experienced the application process as a parent and trusted confidante to a group of young men (and one young woman belatedly). My only hope is that these reflections offer some helpful context for everyone involved: students, parents, carers, schools, and universities alike.

The Denouement

The denouement is that all but one of the young men – who has deferred his engineering place at Kingston – are about to set off for university. One is heading to Loughborough to study sports science, another to King’s College London for geography, another to Northeastern University London for philosophy and another to Westminster for biology.

All’s well that ends well.

Yet I’m well aware that some of these outcomes depended on a dollop of good luck. Institutions vary enormously in how much support they offer and how accessible they are; a family without someone able to counsel, chase, call, and insist could easily have seen a very different result. While these five young men certainly engaged, they also benefited from an immense amount of effort put in on their behalf by their school, by the universities and by me. Not every applicant this autumn will be so fortunate.

title: How College Essays Have Changed—and Stayed the Same
summary:
How College Essays Have Changed—and Stayed the Same
Johanna Alonso Wed, 09/09/2026 - 03:00 AM

Ethan Sawyer began his coaching business in 2012 and keeps close track of admission writing prompts. Despite yearly fuss over changing prompts, he says the college essay of today is much the same as it was over a decade ago.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
Screenwriting and college essay coaching aren’t all that different, according to Ethan Sawyer.

Sawyer, who has spent more than two decades helping students get into college, mostly under the pseudonym College Essay Guy, holds two theater degrees and dreamed of writing movies but fell into coaching admissions essays as his first job out of college. Quickly, he noticed an unlikely connection between the two fields.

“[I was] taking what I was learning from screenwriting, those storytelling principles, and incorporating them into my work with students,” he said. “I always knew that I loved having deep conversations with people, and I knew that I liked helping people solve problems. But suddenly, I realized, ‘Oh, this actually is something that brings together a lot of my interests and skills.’”

Sawyer started his own company in 2012, and, in recent years, has also begun filling a niche in the admissions world: He tracks supplemental essays, including which institutions require them and what types of prompts are most common. He believes that he might be the single person in the nation who is most tapped in to these prompts. That attention has made him an asset not only to his clients but also to other college counselors, to whom he offers pay-what-you-can webinars on all things essays.

This admission season marks his fifth tracking those prompts and his 14th as the College Essay Guy. He spoke to Inside Higher Ed about what has changed about college essays over the course of his career, what this year’s essay landscape looks like and more. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: Over the 14 years you’ve been doing this, what are the biggest changes you’ve noticed, both in what colleges are asking for and also in how students feel about the process?

A: I honestly think a lot of it is similar to how it’s been from years past. I think there’s a lot of focus and talk about how things are quote-unquote always changing, but when I think about what this process is at a fundamental level, it’s students digging deep to figure out what are the parts of myself that I can show to colleges alongside the hard work that I put in to get good grades, to challenge myself. But I think the process, to me, is more similar to what it was 15 years ago than different.

I think a big thing happened around when a lot of institutions went to test optional and test blind. Everybody sort of shifted and went, “OK, what really matters now?” I think there was an increased interest in the college essay, the written parts of the application, because students were like, “Well, that’s how I’m going to differentiate myself.” My sense of it is that sort of stayed, even though some selective schools have [reinstated testing requirements]. Colleges are still really interested in that, and I’ve been really checking, asking admission officers, “Do you sense that essays are going away?” And nobody that I’ve ever talked to on the admission side has said, “Yeah, I can see where that’s potentially happening.”

Q: One thing that I hear from other people in the admissions counseling world is about anxiety: the feeling that student anxiety and pressure on themselves has increased. Is that something you sense, and how have you dealt with that?

A: I think after COVID—and I saw this with my own daughter, who did her first day of school online in kindergarten—I think kids were staying inside more, obviously, and even my own daughter didn’t want to go out as much. She was like, “I kind of want to stay home, because it’s cozy here and it’s safe.”

What I saw is more students were writing about anxiety, and when I talk to admission officers and I ask them, “What are the most common topics that you see?” it’s anxiety. It has sort of replaced the essay that used to be the big cliché, [which] is students doing the mission trip, going somewhere else, working with people who have relatively less money, less privilege, and then making an impact on their lives. That’s become more cringe, to use their term, but what’s replaced it is this focus on and thinking about mental health and anxiety.

I think that for many students—this is just, like, me getting into College Essay Guy–mode for a second—they feel like they should write about that in their personal statement. I think that there’s opportunities for them to put that in the “challenges and circumstances” section, I think there are opportunities for them to have their counselor write about that, and then also students should just know that they don’t have to put that in their personal statement. That could just be a journey that they went through, and that may not be the best way to show their skills, qualities and values. But oftentimes for students, that challenge looms so large because it’s the biggest thing that they’ve been dealing with.

Q: Regarding AI, I’m curious about what you see on your end. When students first come to you, are they asking you whether they can use AI? Have they already had AI help them?

A: This is fresh for me, because I had two instances in the last 24 hours about this. The thing that I’m doing, the thing I’m encouraging counselors to do, is just to ask and have an open conversation about it and not to load it too much with the moral rightness or wrongness of it. I think there’s that tendency in some circles to be like, “You’re bad if you do it, and you’re taking the moral high ground if you don’t.” I think there’s another move here where we can just sort of go, “Hey, this is a tool. Let’s let it into the room and talk about it.” One of my colleagues asks students at the start of the process, “How do you plan to use AI in your in your application process?” It opens up a dialogue. So, I just want to really encourage counselors to normalize it as much as we can.

I talked to 20 college admission reps [about this], and they were like, “Don’t. Really, just don’t,” really taking a hard-line stance. For now, we take the position of, we don’t encourage you to use it for writing. We do think it can be really useful for researching. Make sure that you ask it for links. But the Common App says it really needs to be your own work, so make sure that it is. And then the other piece that I think is important is I really want students to feel like, if an admission officer asks them, “How did you use AI in your process?” I really want them to feel proud of their answer.

Q: I wanted to talk about your Matchlighters program, where counselors work pro bono with low-income, high-achieving students. How did that come to be and what has that experience been like?

A: I was working in, like, test prep before I became College Essay Guy, and I met a guy who ran a charter school in Los Angeles, and he was like, “Hey, would you ever be willing to come and teach test prep for my students?” So I sort of started volunteering there with my best friend, and then I was like, “Can we do essay stuff, too?” So, we created this program where we would do test prep in the winter into the spring, and then we would do college essays in the fall, a sort of boot camp–style thing, and we did that for a few years, and we expanded that to five different charter schools in the L.A. area.

So, when I started CEG, students were reaching out, like, “Hey, can I get some support?” And I would do some stuff for free. I would encourage them to join my courses, and, from day one, all of the courses were pay-what-you-can. In 2015, a student emailed me and was like, “Hey, I’m a high-achieving, low-income student. I just need someone to light a little match.” So I just put on a spreadsheet 20 or so students that I’d heard from, and then I reached out to my counselor email list and was like, “Hey, does anybody want to volunteer with students?” I think it was like 25 or something raised their hand, and I just matched them up on a spreadsheet. That just grew over the years, and in this past year, we matched almost 800 students and counselors on a one-to-one basis.

We’ve just had incredible experiences and results. We’ve had years where like 10 students got into Harvard, or 12 students got into Yale.

Q: Are there any particular lessons from doing the Matchlighters program that have particularly informed how you think about your work over all?

A: Students who come from low-income backgrounds have often faced a lot of challenges in their lives, and I think that when students read essays that are impactful, they sort of see a big challenge, and they’re like, “OK, I need to talk about my challenge.” What I’ve seen over the years is that there are a lot of ways to do that that don’t necessarily involve focusing on the challenge, but incorporating it. I guess my hope for students who have faced challenges in life is that they do some brainstorming around, “What are the other parts of myself that I want to bring, so that I’m not defined by this—that it’s part of me, but it’s not all of who I am?”

I’ve seen over the years there’s more range and possibilities and variety of what’s possible there in terms of telling a story. It’s not like you just write about the challenge or you don’t write about the challenge; there are ways of weaving it in, and that’s become more and more clear to me over the years.

This work of access is not that hard. When an independent educational consultant is thinking about, “Who do I work with?” obviously there is a tendency to want to work with people who can pay for it, because that’s what keeps the lights on. But I want to say, adding an element of pro bono work that is commensurate with the work that you’re doing for paying clients is just a matter of some planning. That’s one of the things that I’ve realized over the years. The message I want to give is, like, it’s easier than you think to do something like this. If folks are interested in learning more about how to do that, we as an organization would be really willing to talk to folks about doing that, and we’ve got resources on how to do that.

Q: Tracking supplemental essay prompts has become a big part of what you do in the past five years. What’s new this year in supplemental essays and what have you learned over the past several years?

A: There are [not many] schools asking about using AI in the process. Villanova added one, but out of the 300 prompts, that’s it. There aren’t actually more schools, which was surprising, because I would have expected more schools to be asking about that, but that didn’t change. That’s in a category of things that I expected to change more that didn’t. Another one is I’ve expected over the years—like five to 10 years—more schools to be adding video components. But they haven’t. When I ask admission officers about why, they say a couple things. One is, you can’t skim an interview. Like, “We’re reading really fast, we don’t have time to really take in a video.” So, it’s a scaling thing. And then I think people are still thinking a little bit about access

The “why major” [prompt]—that one’s stayed pretty similar over the years and is usually [used by] colleges that admit by major or that somehow helps them decide where to slot students in. I’m surprised there aren’t more colleges that have short-answer questions, because I think that that is a fun way to get into students’ personality really quickly. The “navigating adversity” one really started to become more popular after [widespread campus protests in 2023 and 2024]. The theme seems to be around bridge-building; NYU specifically calls out bridge-building. And I just think that that’s just such a beautiful essence for what college is all about anyway, so it is pointing to core values more than just, they’re afraid and they want to attract the students who are not going to riot.

title: Studyportals and Made Impact partner to showcase personal international education stories
summary:
Studyportals and Made Impact have partnered to launch a global platform designed to collect and amplify stories demonstrating the impact of international education and student mobility.

The post Studyportals and Made Impact partner to showcase personal international education stories appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The Impactportal was unveiled at the inaugural Made Impact Summit, held at the United Nations in New York on September 1, bringing together education leaders, policymakers and storytellers focused on strengthening the case for international education and exchange.

The partnership combines Studyportals’ reach and expertise in international higher education with Made Impact’s storytelling and movement-building capabilities.

The organisations said the Impactportal will provide a collaborative space to showcase the human, societal and economic impact of international education, student mobility and global talent.

Meanwhile, Studyportals CEO Edwin van Rest will join Made Impact as a co-founding leader of the initiative.

“International education changes lives every day, yet too often its impact remains invisible or difficult to quantify,” van Rest said.

International education changes lives every day, yet too often its impact remains invisible or difficult to quantify

Edwin van Rest, Studyportals

“Announcing this partnership at the United Nations reflects the scale of our ambition. Through the Impactportal, we want to bring together compelling stories and credible evidence from around the world, helping institutions, governments and communities better understand the profound value of international education.”

Chris Arnold, founder of Made Impact, said international education and exchange represented a long-term strategy for maximising human potential and supporting prosperity and peace.

“We want to build a sector-inclusive movement, and therefore partnering with a powerhouse in the education space, Studyportals, with a mission so aligned to ours, is a big win for us, and for the world,” he said.

The Impactportal will become a global repository of stories from universities, students, alumni and partners, enabling them to share experiences and demonstrate the broader effects of international education.

The initiative comes amid significant challenges for global international education as institutions across major markets grapple with compliance squeezes, anti-immigration rhetoric and questions about higher education’s relevance in an AI-driven world.

In response, the partners said the platform will seek to combine personal stories with evidence to build a stronger and more visible narrative around the value of international education.

Meanwhile, the summit followed a storyteller day on Ellis Island, where participants from across the international education sector explored how personal stories can help capture the impact of studying, working and living across cultures.

The two-day program brought together voices from different countries, careers and backgrounds, with discussions spanning human potential, prosperity and peace, as Made Impact works towards its ambition of collecting one million stories demonstrating the impact of international education and exchange.

The focus comes at a time when the sector is under growing pressure to articulate its value beyond student numbers and economic contribution, and to show the wider human impact of international experiences.

title: Datenschutz als Katalysator der Hochschuldigitalisierung
summary:
Digitalisierung verändert Prozesse im Hochschulalltag. Hochschulen werden von den Entwicklungen in der Gesellschaft überrollt, wenn sie keinen adäquaten Umgang damit finden.

The post Datenschutz als Katalysator der Hochschuldigitalisierung appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Datenschutzbeauftragte können bei der Transformation eine Schnittstellenfunktion übernehmen. Ihre Stärke liegt darin, Perspektiven und praktische Erfahrungen aus mehreren Anwendungsgebieten einzubringen und beratend an tragfähigen Lösungen mitwirken.

Denn sie haben Einblicke in viele Prozesse. Häufig ist ihr Wissen nicht auf Datenschutzrecht beschränkt, so dass sie fachübergreifend Denkanstöße geben können.

Digitalisierung führt zu ähnlichen Herausforderungen. Wenn ein Verfahren einmal sorgfältig geprüft und praxistauglich ausgestaltet wurde, kann daraus ein hochschulübergreifender Standard entstehen.

Aus einem Einzelfall wird Erfahrungswissen. Aus Erfahrungswissen entstehen Best Practices.

Häufig wiederholt sich ein bekanntes Muster: Es wird eine Software gesucht, die etablierte Abläufe abbildet, Produkte werden verglichen, technische Anforderungen definiert und möglicherweise bereits Verträge geschlossen.

Erst im Nachgang wird geklärt, inwieweit rechtliche Anforderungen erfüllt und ob Vereinfachungen der Prozesse denkbar wären. Dann wird es schwierig. Technische Strukturen stehen bereits fest, Beschaffungsentscheidungen sind weit gediehen und Anpassungen kosten Zeit und Geld.

Sinnvoller ist es deshalb, Datenschutz und darüber hinaus gehende Compliance von Anfang an mitzudenken. Genau diesem Gedanken folgt Privacy by Design: Rechtliche und technische Anforderungen sollen nicht gegeneinander ausgespielt, sondern von vornherein gemeinsam in die Konzeption integriert werden.

Die Datenschutzgrundverordnung erwartet eine frühzeitige Einbindung der Datenschutzbeauftragten (s. Art. 38f DSGVO), so dass sie nicht mehr nur fertige Konzepte prüfen, sondern Projekte bereits in der Entwicklungsphase begleiten, Alternativen aufzeigen, Erfahrungen weitergeben und Risiken benennen können.

KI-Anwendungen sind ein typisches Querschnittsthema und werfen Fragen zu Lehre, Prüfungen, Urheberrecht, Datenschutz sowie zur guten wissenschaftlichen Praxis auf.

Generative KI ist längst in Studium und Lehre angekommen. Lehrende nutzen sie zur Vorbereitung von Veranstaltungen, Studierende verwenden Sprachmodelle beim Schreiben, Programmieren und Lernen. Häufig werden dafür kommerzielle Angebote genutzt, während andere Open Source Modelle nutzen.

Relevante Fragen sind:

Für welche Zwecke wollen wir KI nutzen und wo ziehen wir bewusst Grenzen?

Welche Daten dürfen eingegeben werden?

Wohin werden die Daten übertragen und wer hat auf sie Zugriff?

Wie transparent soll die Nutzung sein?

Dabei kommen mehrere Perspektiven zusammen, wie die Empfehlungen der Universität Bremen zeigen – neben technischen Aspekten müssen didaktische, rechtliche und ethische Fragen betrachtet werden.

Datenschutzbeauftragte können auf bekannte Lösungsansätze verweisen. Und falls neben Datenschutz Informationssicherheit, Prüfungs- und Urheberrecht oder die europäische Digitalregulierung eine Rolle spielen, auch darauf.

Sie müssen dafür nicht zwangsläufig zu KI-Beauftragten werden. Entscheidend ist vielmehr, relevante Fragen früh zu diskutieren und die richtigen Personen zusammenbringen.

Noch deutlicher zeigt sich diese Vermittlerrolle beim Forschungsdatenmanagement.

Moderne Forschung setzt auf Nachvollziehbarkeit, Nachnutzbarkeit und möglichst offene Daten. Gleichzeitig können Forschungsdaten sensible Informationen über Menschen enthalten. Hinzu kommen Fragen zu Urheberrechten, Kooperationen, Drittmittelbedingungen und ethischen Anforderungen.

Auch hier hilft ein einfaches „Ja“ oder „Nein“ kaum weiter. Die entscheidende Frage lautet:

Wie können Forschungsdaten so organisiert werden, dass Forschung ermöglicht und zugleich ein verantwortungsvoller Umgang mit den Daten gewährleistet wird?

Das beginnt oft schon bei der Planung eines Forschungsprojekts. Welche Daten werden tatsächlich benötigt und wie werden sie strukturiert? Wann können sie anonymisiert oder pseudonymisiert werden? Welche Daten können später veröffentlicht oder nachgenutzt werden?

Die Forschungsdaten-Policy der Freien Universität Berlin zeigt beispielhaft, wie Forschungsdatenmanagement, gute wissenschaftliche Praxis, Open Science, Datenschutz und Informationssicherheit zusammengedacht werden können. Auch das Informationsportal forschungsdaten.info verbindet Forschungsdatenmanagement mit den rechtlichen Rahmenbedingungen personenbezogener Forschungsdaten.

Datenschutzbeauftragte sind Ansprechpersonen für personenbezogene Forschungsprojekte. Gleichzeitig lernen sie aus unterschiedlichen Projekten. Ein Lösungsansatz für eine Befragungsstudie kann für ein anderes Forschungsvorhaben adaptiert werden. Erfahrungen mit Pseudonymisierung oder Treuhandmodellen sind übertragbar.

Damit wird Datenschutzberatung zugleich zu Wissensmanagement.

Dieser Gedanke lässt sich auf viele Digitalisierungsthemen übertragen.

Cloud-Dienste, Videokonferenzen, Lernplattformen, KI-Anwendungen oder Identitätsmanagement stellen Hochschulen immer wieder vor ähnliche Fragen. Trotzdem werden Lösungen häufig dezentral und unabhängig voneinander entwickelt.

Das ist angesichts knapper Ressourcen wenig effizient.

Datenschutzbeauftragte verfügen aufgrund ihrer hochschulweiten Tätigkeit über einen besonderen Überblick. Sie sehen ähnliche Fragestellungen an verschiedenen Stellen. Sie kennen bereits geprüfte Verfahren und typische Fehler. Sie wissen, welche Ansätze andernorts gut funktionieren und welche nicht.

Sie helfen, Wissen zu systematisieren. Muster, Handreichungen und Checklisten sind das Eine, sie können aber nicht die persönliche Beratung ersetzen. Ebenso wichtig ist aber die informelle Funktion: Menschen miteinander in Kontakt bringen, auf Erfahrungen ausnutzen und vermeiden, dass sich Fehler wiederholen.

Genau darin liegt die Stärke von Datenschutzbeauftragten. Als unabhängige Instanz können sie die Digitalisierung beflügeln.

Der Wissenstransfer sollte dabei nicht an der Hochschulgrenze enden.

Eine Berliner Universität steht beim Einsatz von KI, Cloud-Diensten oder Lernsoftware häufig vor ähnlichen Fragen wie andere Hochschulen von Flensburg bis Passau. Viele Lösungen lassen sich zumindest teilweise übertragen.

Deshalb sind regionale und bundesweite Netzwerke besonders wertvoll. Sie können Keimzellen gemeinsamer Lösungen sein.

Aus der Erfahrung einer einzelnen Hochschule kann dort eine breite Diskussion entstehen. Andere Hochschulen bringen ihre Perspektiven ein, Unterschiede werden sichtbar und Lösungsansätze werden weiterentwickelt. Im besten Fall entsteht daraus eine Best Practice, die anschließend wieder in die einzelnen Hochschulen zurückwirkt.

Das 2025 gegründete deutschlandweite Netzwerk Hochschuldatenschutz knüpft genau hier an. Es ergänzt bestehende regionale Netzwerke und etablierte Strukturen und schafft Raum für den Austausch über hochschultypische Themen mit Datenschutzbezug wie Student-Lifecycle-Management aber auch allgemeine Themen wie Cybersecurity.

Solche Netzwerke sind mehr als reine Austauschforen. Sie tragen dazu bei, knappe Ressourcen besser einzusetzen und bewährte Lösungen zu verbreiten.

Mit zunehmender Digitalisierung verschwimmen klassische Zuständigkeitsgrenzen.

In der Regel sind sowohl Datenschutz und Informationssicherheit, häufig aber auch Urheber- und Prüfungsrecht als auch KI-Regulierung relevant. Bei Forschungsprojekten kommen Ethik und Exportkontrolle hinzu. Bei neuen Verwaltungsverfahren sind Prozessmanagement, IT, Personalvertretung und Compliance betroffen.

Keine einzelne Stelle kann all diese Aufgaben übernehmen. Bessere Zusammenarbeit ist der Schlüssel zum Erfolg.

Datenschutzbeauftragte können dabei als eine Art regulatorischer Sensor wirken. Aufgrund ihrer Querschnittstätigkeit erkennen sie frühzeitig, wenn ein Vorhaben nicht nur datenschutzrechtliche Fragen aufwirft. Sie können andere Stakeholder einbeziehen und dazu beitragen, unterschiedliche Anforderungen zusammenzuführen.

Das Ziel sollte eine Digital Governance sein, in der Fachlichkeit, Technik, Recht und Organisation nicht nebeneinander, sondern gemeinsam betrachtet werden.

Dabei bleibt eine wichtige Grenze bestehen.

Datenschutzbeauftragte dürfen nicht selbst die Prozesse verantworten, die sie unabhängig kontrollieren sollen. Die Hochschulleitung und die verantwortlichen Organisationseinheiten müssen entscheiden und die Umsetzung verantworten. Die Leitlinien der europäischen Datenschutzbehörden zur Rolle der Datenschutzbeauftragten betonen deshalb sowohl die Beratungs- und Vermittlungsfunktion als auch die unabhängige Stellung der Datenschutzbeauftragten.

Das bedeutet aber nicht, dass Datenschutzbeauftragte Abstand zu Digitalisierungsprojekten halten müssten.

Im Gegenteil.

Sie können Projekte intensiv begleiten, Alternativen diskutieren, bewährte Lösungen vermitteln und auch deutlich widersprechen, wenn Risiken aus ihrer Sicht nicht vertretbar sind.

Unabhängigkeit bedeutet Autonomie in der fachlichen Bewertung, nicht Distanz zum Projekt.

Das passende Leitbild lautet daher: kritische Nähe statt distanzierter Kontrolle.

Das klassische Bild vom Datenschutz als Bremse der Digitalisierung greift damit zu kurz.

Schlecht organisierter Datenschutz kann Prozesse tatsächlich verzögern. Das gilt vor allem dann, wenn er erst bedacht wird, nachdem wesentliche Entscheidungen bereits gefallen sind.

Frühzeitige, lösungsorientierte Datenschutzberatung kann dagegen das Gegenteil bewirken.

Sie hilft, Anforderungen früh zu erkennen. Sie vermeidet spätere Korrekturen. Sie bringt Erfahrungen aus anderen Projekten ein. Sie verbindet Fachleute und kann dazu beitragen, aus einzelnen Lösungen wiederverwendbare Standards zu entwickeln.

Datenschutzbeauftragte sind deshalb weder Digitalisierungsverantwortlichen einer Hochschule noch Compliance-Manager. Sie sind Schnittstelle, Wissensträger und Multiplikatoren. In regionalen und bundesweiten Netzwerken können sie Erfahrungen über die eigene Hochschule hinaus weitergeben und gemeinsam weiterentwickeln.

So verstanden werden Datenschutzbeauftragte zu Katalysatoren der Digitalisierung.

title: La scuola ha digitalizzato le aule. Ora deve proteggere l’attenzione
summary:
Smartphone, piattaforme e intelligenza artificiale ampliano le opportunità educative, ma incidono su attenzione, relazioni e benessere. Alla scuola spetta integrare il digitale nella didattica e insegnare agli studenti a gestirlo con consapevolezza, oltre divieti e competenze tecniche

L'articolo La scuola ha digitalizzato le aule. Ora deve proteggere l’attenzione proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
Il dibattito sull’innovazione digitale nella scuola si è concentrato, finora, soprattutto sulle opportunità offerte dalle tecnologie educative: personalizzazione dell’apprendimento, accesso a contenuti digitali, ambienti collaborativi online e strumenti di supporto per docenti e studenti. Tuttavia, accanto a queste opportunità sta emergendo con sempre maggiore forza una questione altrettanto rilevante: il rapporto tra uso delle tecnologie e benessere degli studenti.

La diffusione massiva di dispositivi digitali nella vita quotidiana dei giovani ha modificato profondamente le modalità di apprendimento, comunicazione e socializzazione. Smartphone, piattaforme social, ambienti digitali di studio e strumenti basati sull’intelligenza artificiale accompagnano ormai gran parte delle attività educative. In questo contesto, la scuola non può limitarsi a introdurre tecnologie, ma deve interrogarsi su come promuovere un uso equilibrato e consapevole degli strumenti digitali.

Digital wellbeing nella scuola e benessere degli studenti

Le ricerche internazionali mostrano che l’impatto delle tecnologie sul benessere degli studenti è complesso e dipende da molte variabili: modalità di utilizzo, contesto educativo, età degli studenti e qualità delle interazioni sociali. In alcuni casi le tecnologie digitali possono favorire l’accesso alla conoscenza e la collaborazione tra studenti; in altri, un uso eccessivo o non regolato può contribuire a fenomeni di sovraccarico cognitivo, distrazione o riduzione dell’attenzione (OECD, Students, Digital Devices and Learning). Il problema non è la tecnologia in sé, ma il modo in cui viene integrata nei processi educativi.

Il concetto di digital wellbeing nasce proprio per affrontare questa complessità. Non si tratta di limitare l’uso delle tecnologie, ma di sviluppare un equilibrio tra attività digitali, relazioni sociali e benessere psicologico. Le istituzioni internazionali sottolineano che la scuola deve svolgere un ruolo centrale nella costruzione di queste competenze, aiutando gli studenti a comprendere gli effetti delle tecnologie sulla propria attenzione, sul tempo di studio e sulla qualità delle relazioni (UNESCO, Digital Wellbeing in Education).

Gestione dell’attenzione e tempo digitale

Un elemento particolarmente rilevante riguarda la capacità di gestire l’attenzione in un ambiente informativo caratterizzato da stimoli continui. Notifiche, messaggi, contenuti multimediali e piattaforme social competono costantemente per catturare l’attenzione degli utenti. In questo contesto, la gestione consapevole del tempo digitale diventa una competenza educativa fondamentale. Gli studenti devono imparare a riconoscere le dinamiche che influenzano la loro concentrazione e a sviluppare strategie per mantenere un rapporto equilibrato con le tecnologie.

Il digital wellbeing riguarda anche la dimensione emotiva e relazionale. Le piattaforme digitali amplificano le possibilità di comunicazione ma possono anche generare nuove forme di pressione sociale, confronto continuo e dipendenza dalle dinamiche dei social media. La scuola ha quindi la responsabilità di sviluppare percorsi educativi che aiutino gli studenti a comprendere queste dinamiche e a costruire un rapporto critico e consapevole con gli ambienti digitali.

Educazione digitale, cittadinanza e politiche europee

Le politiche educative europee stanno iniziando a riconoscere questa dimensione. Il Digital Education Action Plan evidenzia la necessità di promuovere competenze che combinino uso delle tecnologie, cittadinanza digitale e benessere degli studenti (European Commission, Digital Education Action Plan). In questa prospettiva, l’educazione digitale non può limitarsi all’acquisizione di competenze tecniche, ma deve includere anche la capacità di gestire l’impatto delle tecnologie sulla vita quotidiana.

In definitiva, l’innovazione digitale nella scuola non può essere valutata solo in termini di strumenti o piattaforme. La qualità dell’esperienza educativa dipende anche dalla capacità di integrare le tecnologie in modo sostenibile e rispettoso del benessere degli studenti.

Se il digital wellbeing diventa una dimensione centrale dell’educazione contemporanea, allora la scuola è chiamata a sviluppare strategie concrete per integrare il benessere digitale nei percorsi formativi. Non si tratta di introdurre semplici regole sull’uso dei dispositivi, ma di costruire un’educazione alla consapevolezza digitale capace di aiutare gli studenti a comprendere il funzionamento degli ambienti tecnologici in cui vivono.

Strategie concrete per il digital wellbeing a scuola

Uno dei primi ambiti di intervento riguarda la gestione dell’attenzione. Le tecnologie digitali sono progettate per massimizzare l’interazione degli utenti, attraverso notifiche, contenuti personalizzati e sistemi di raccomandazione. In un contesto educativo, questo può entrare in tensione con la necessità di sviluppare concentrazione e riflessione approfondita. Per questo motivo molte ricerche suggeriscono di introdurre nelle scuole percorsi educativi dedicati alla gestione del tempo digitale e alla consapevolezza delle dinamiche dell’attenzione (OECD, Students, Digital Devices and Learning).

Un secondo elemento riguarda la dimensione sociale delle tecnologie. Le piattaforme digitali hanno ampliato le opportunità di comunicazione tra studenti, ma hanno anche introdotto nuove forme di pressione sociale e dinamiche relazionali complesse. La scuola può svolgere un ruolo importante nel promuovere competenze di cittadinanza digitale, aiutando gli studenti a comprendere il funzionamento dei social media, le implicazioni della propria identità online e l’importanza di comportamenti responsabili negli ambienti digitali (Council of Europe, Digital Citizenship Education).

Tecnologie digitali, metodologie didattiche e AI

Un ulteriore aspetto riguarda l’integrazione tra tecnologie digitali e metodologie didattiche. L’uso di strumenti digitali non deve tradursi in un aumento indiscriminato del tempo trascorso davanti agli schermi. Le esperienze più efficaci sono quelle che alternano attività digitali e attività in presenza, momenti di lavoro individuale e collaborazione tra studenti. Il digitale diventa uno strumento al servizio dell’apprendimento, non un ambiente totalizzante. Questa integrazione permette di sfruttare i vantaggi delle tecnologie mantenendo al centro le relazioni educative.

La crescente diffusione dell’intelligenza artificiale rende il tema del benessere digitale ancora più rilevante. Gli strumenti basati su AI possono supportare l’apprendimento personalizzato e offrire nuove forme di tutoraggio, ma possono anche generare un’interazione sempre più continua tra studenti e sistemi digitali. Per questo motivo diverse istituzioni internazionali sottolineano la necessità di sviluppare modelli di AI educativa che rispettino i principi del benessere e della sostenibilità cognitiva (UNESCO, AI and Education: Guidance for Policy-Makers).

Le politiche educative stanno iniziando a riconoscere questa dimensione. Il Digital Education Action Plan invita i sistemi educativi europei a promuovere un approccio equilibrato all’innovazione tecnologica, in cui lo sviluppo delle competenze digitali sia accompagnato da attenzione al benessere degli studenti e alla qualità delle relazioni educative (European Commission, Digital Education Action Plan). L’obiettivo è costruire ambienti di apprendimento in cui tecnologia e benessere non siano in conflitto, ma si rafforzino reciprocamente.

Formazione dei docenti e innovazione educativa

Un ruolo fondamentale è svolto anche dalla formazione dei docenti. Gli insegnanti devono essere preparati non solo all’uso delle tecnologie, ma anche alla gestione delle dinamiche cognitive e relazionali che queste generano. Comprendere quando e come utilizzare gli strumenti digitali, come favorire la concentrazione degli studenti e come promuovere un uso consapevole delle tecnologie diventa parte integrante della professionalità docente.
